content: Biomechanics applies principles of mechanics to biological systems, analyzing forces and their effects on the body during movement. In skateboarding, these principles determine both performance capabilities and injury risks. The conservation of energy principle explains how skateboarders convert potential energy (proportional to height) to kinetic energy (proportional to velocity squared) when descending ramps. This conversion is nearly frictionless on well-designed surfaces, allowing riders to reach approximately the same height on opposite ends of a halfpipe. Newton's laws govern skateboard motion: the first law explains why riders maintain forward motion without continuous pushing; the second law (F=ma) describes how force from pushing or gravity produces acceleration; the third law underlies the equal and opposite forces between wheels and surfaces. Angular momentum conservation enables aerial rotationsâonce airborne, skaters adjust body position to control rotation speed, similar to figure skaters pulling in their arms to spin faster. Impact forces follow the impulse-momentum relationship, where force Ã time = mass Ã velocity change. This explains why skateboarders bend their knees when landing to extend impact time and reduce peak forces. Materials science affects performance through board flexibility (affecting pop and energy return) and wheel composition (determining grip and vibration damping). Ergonomics principles guide optimal board dimensions for different rider sizes and styles, while biomechanical load analysis helps identify high-stress body positions that may lead to acute or chronic injuries.

scenario.title: Skatepark Engineering Lab
scenario.content: Students design skateparks using engineering tools that incorporate biomechanical analysis of rider movements. The simulation allows manipulation of ramp dimensions, transitions, materials, and surface properties while providing real-time physics feedback. Students can place virtual riders on their creations to visualize forces acting on the body throughout various maneuvers, with color-coded stress indicators for different anatomical structures. The system calculates and displays potential energy, kinetic energy, momentum, impact forces, and center of mass trajectories during simulated runs. Interactive tools enable students to modify rider technique, board characteristics, and protective equipment to observe effects on performance and safety metrics. Challenge modes task students with designing park features that optimize for specific objectives like trick progression, injury prevention, or accessibility for riders with different skill levels.

hypothesis.description: Students will apply biomechanical principles to engineered environments by analyzing how physical structures interact with biological systems. They will predict how design choices affect human movement patterns and forces, and create solutions that optimize for both performance enhancement and injury prevention.
